Canada reconnaît la Palestine : pourquoi: Canada recognizes Palestine: why Quebec’s Palestinian community remains skeptical
Dans sa déclaration de reconnaissance, M: In his declaration of recognition, Mr. Carney proposed “a partnership to build the promise of a peaceful future”
Manifestation à Montréal en soutien au p: Demonstration in Montréal in support of the people of Gaza. Photo credit: Édouard Desroches
La nouvelle de la reconnaissance de la P: The news that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney had recognized Palestine raised many questions about what this means for the Palestinian community in Quebec. After discussing the recognition with several Palestinians of different ages and backgrounds, I noticed that they all shared the same feelings. Since Mr. Carney has still taken no action to end the genocide or stop sending the weapons that allow Israel to attack the population of Gaza, these people reject his declaration. For them, recognition without an arms embargo is nothing but a façade. I hope the perspectives presented here will offer new insights.
<strong>Le mardi 7 octobre, deux ans apr: On Tuesday, October 7, two years after the start of Israel’s genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, thousands of students from universities across Quebec walked out of their classes in solidarity with Palestine. Gathered in front of Concordia University’s Hall Building, they then marched to McGill University to demand that their institutions divest.
Quelques semaines plus tôt, le premier m: A few weeks earlier, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney had officially recognized the State of Palestine. We took the time to speak with Palestinians in Quebec to gather their reactions to the announcement. Many see the recognition as a symbolic gesture, disconnected from the reality lived by the people of Gaza.
Dans sa déclaration de reconnaissance, M: In his declaration of recognition, Mr. Carney proposed “a partnership to build the promise of a peaceful future for both the State of Palestine and the State of Israel.” He also confirmed that the Palestinian Authority had made “direct commitments” to Canada in response to its demands. Many Palestinians consider those demands contradictory to the very concept of recognition.
<strong>« Ce n’est pas seulement un gest: “It’s not just a meaningless gesture, it’s actually misleading”
Haya Alsakka, une Palestinienne de Gaza: Haya Alsakka, a Palestinian from Gaza who works as an organizer with the Palestinian Youth Movement in Montréal, remembers feeling disappointed and frustrated when she heard the news of Canada’s recognition of Palestine. She points out that the recognition comes with no conditions aimed at ending the genocide, lifting the siege of Gaza, or stopping the growing annexations in the West Bank and the illegal occupation of Palestinian territories.
« De manière réaliste, et surtout en pér: “Realistically, and especially in a time of genocide, it’s not just a meaningless gesture, it’s actually misleading. It’s meant to divert attention from the call for an arms embargo and to soften Canada’s image on the international stage,” says Ms<sup>.</sup> Alsakka.
Elle souligne qu’au cours des deux derni: She notes that over the past two years, there have been clear calls for Canada to impose a bilateral arms embargo on Israel and end its complicity in the ongoing genocide, which makes this recognition “a bad-faith effort to stifle that call.”
M<sup>me</sup> Alsakka remarque égalemen: Ms<sup>.</sup> Alsakka also observes that pressure on the government is mounting, as Canada’s involvement in the war crimes committed by Israel against Palestinians has been increasingly exposed in recent months. She refers to a recent report published by the Palestinian Youth Movement in collaboration with other organizations taking part in the Arms Embargo Now campaign, which denounces Canada’s military exports to Israel.
Les conclusions de ce <l1>rapport</l1> é: The findings of this <l1>report</l1> establish that Canada never stopped sending weapons to Israel, revealing the Canadian government’s denial of its involvement in the genocide. The authors used complementary methodologies to track arms exports and isolated three trade channels: direct commercial exports from Canadian companies to Israel, indirect exports of Canadian weapons to Israel via the United States, and imports of Israeli military technology and equipment.
Affaires mondiales Canada a déclaré qu’a: Global Affairs Canada has stated that no export permits for weapons that could be used in Gaza have been approved since January 2024. In addition, Canadian Minister of Foreign Affairs Mélanie Joly has said that about thirty permits have been suspended since then. However, according to the analysis carried out for the report, 47 shipments were made by Canadian manufacturers to Israeli manufacturers between October 2023 and July 2025, under previously approved permits.
Le rapport divulgue d’autres information: The report discloses other important information about Canada’s arms trade with Israel. This includes the Canadian companies and the parts essential to the continuation of Israel’s daily attacks on Gaza, the quantity and types of military equipment shipped and how that equipment is used against Palestinians, as well as other inferences based on the data that could be retrieved.
M<sup>me</sup> Alsakka estime que ces re: Ms<sup>.</sup> Alsakka believes this research must be widely promoted and expanded so that the public continues to question the Canadian government’s claims about its role in perpetrating this genocide, and keeps pressing for an arms embargo.
« Nous avons des preuves très concrètes: “We have very concrete evidence that our government has allowed and facilitated the flow of weapons to the State of Israel, and that Israel could not have carried out this genocide without those weapons. We need to redouble our efforts to demand [an arms embargo] and to demand an immediate ceasefire, because Canada has the power to do so,” she adds.
<strong>« Malgré cette reconnaissance, G: “Despite this recognition, Gaza continues to be bombed”
Nayrouz Abu Hatoum est Palestinienne. El: Nayrouz Abu Hatoum is Palestinian. She is an associate professor in the Department of Sociology and Anthropology at Concordia University. Her research focuses on national sovereignty in relation to the Palestinian struggle and the struggle for liberation, particularly in the occupied West Bank. Like many other Palestinians she knows, Ms<sup>.</sup> Abu Hatoum is treating this announcement with extreme skepticism, for many reasons.
Elle attire l’attention sur le fait que: She draws attention to the fact that Mr. Carney said he wants a “Zionist Palestinian state” during his <l1>interview</l1> with Micheal Forman, president of the Council on Foreign Relations. “I found that problematic, to say the least, especially since he is asking a society in the eastern Mediterranean to adopt a 19<sup>th</sup>-century Western European national political movement,” she says.
M<sup>me</sup> Abu Hatoum souligne que l: Ms<sup>.</sup> Abu Hatoum points out that Canada remains complicit in the genocide being carried out by Israel against Palestine, making its declaration tantamount to recognizing a state without a people. “If Israel isn’t stopped, then we’re talking about a weakened state,” she says.
Selon elle, cette reconnaissance n’aura: In her view, this recognition will have no real impact on Palestinians. “Following this recognition, Gaza continues to be bombed. There are still attacks in the West Bank, and Palestinians continue to be victims of ethnic cleansing by settlers. So for Palestinians, this recognition means nothing,” she says.
Un manifestant brandit le drapeau palest: A protester holds up the Palestinian flag in the streets of Montréal. Photo credit: Édouard Desroches
M<sup>me</sup> Abu Hatoum note que deux: Ms<sup>.</sup> Abu Hatoum notes that two readings of Mark Carney’s declaration are currently circulating. The first is that Canada is trying to take control of the pro-Palestinian movement in the country and pretend it has responded to the demands that were made. The second is that the government is trying to offload responsibility for the crimes it has funded and supported.
La professeure conteste un autre élément: The professor challenges another element that Mr. Carney repeats in his declaration, namely the demilitarization of the Palestinian state. She stresses that if Palestinians are deprived of military protection, there is no guarantee that Israel won’t bomb them.
M<sup>me</sup> Abu Hatoum cite le Liban: Ms<sup>.</sup> Abu Hatoum cites Lebanon as another example of a country that Western nations want to demilitarize. “There’s supposed to be a ceasefire. But just yesterday, a family of five was killed, including two children. You want to demilitarize Palestine and Lebanon, but there is no protection,” she explains.
Fort de ce constat, la professeure de l’: Given this, the Concordia University professor foresees the possibility of a new round of negotiations after the failure of the Oslo Accords in 1993, which, she says, will give Israel time, allowing it to buy more time to continue the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians. “By endorsing the creation of a Palestinian state under this model, Western governments simultaneously validate Israel’s right to exist and to expand,” she says.
M<sup>me</sup> Abu Hatoum soutient que,: Ms<sup>.</sup> Abu Hatoum maintains that if the Canadian government respects international law, it should then make clear that Israel cannot defend itself against the peoples it occupies. “They should have done everything in their power to end the genocide. That’s something they haven’t done,” the professor concludes.
<strong>« On ne peut pas faire pression: “You can’t pressure Palestine and then let Israel do as it pleases”
Membre active de la communauté palestini: An active member of Quebec’s Palestinian community, Safiya Barakat teaches history and Arabic. She says she had mixed feelings after hearing the news that Mr. Carney had recognized Palestine. “It’s a right that was stolen from us years and years ago,” she says.
Néanmoins, elle soupçonne que cette reco: Nevertheless, she suspects that the recognition hides certain intentions, given its conditional nature. “It makes no sense to demand the demilitarization of a state whose population is being massacred and starved,” she lets slip.
M<sup>me</sup> Barakat souligne le silen: Ms<sup>.</sup> Barakat points to the silence and inaction of the international community over the years, while Palestinians have been subjected to ethnic cleansing and forcibly displaced from their homes since 1948. “Didn’t the International Criminal Court issue an arrest warrant for Mr. Netanyahu? Why is he still free?” asks the teacher.
Faisant écho aux propos de M<sup>me</sup: Echoing Ms<sup>.</sup> Abu Hatoum’s remarks, she foresees a potential repeat of the Oslo Accords. She denounces the hypocrisy of the conditions imposed by Canada and the imbalance they create. “You can’t pressure Palestine and let Israel do as it pleases,” she says.
Elle considère la déclaration de Mark Ca: She sees Mark Carney’s declaration as a sign of the pressure placed on the Canadian government over the past two years, but also as a strategy to silence the pro-Palestinian community – which is very active in the country – and which has never stopped demanding an end to arms deliveries to Israel.
M<sup>me</sup> Barakat refuse de se sati: Ms<sup>.</sup> Barakat refuses to be satisfied with Canada’s recognition if it is not accompanied by sanctions against Israel and an arms embargo. “If that doesn’t happen, it means their intentions were fraudulent from the start and that they have other plans for Palestine,” she says.
« Pour moi, il n’y a pas de paix sur une: “For me, there is no peace on stolen land. I don’t believe in a two-state solution. And I don’t believe in any form of normalization either. Recognizing [only] Palestine is what would make me happy. It’s my country. It was stolen from us, but it will be free again. We will return. There is no other possibility,” she says.
Léa Pelletier-Marcotte, analyste politiq: Léa Pelletier-Marcotte, a policy analyst at Oxfam-Québec, examines the implications of Mark Carney’s recognition from a humanitarian standpoint.
Elle mentionne que cette reconnaissance: She says the recognition is only the first step in a long list of measures that must be taken to bring about meaningful change on the ground. “This recognition must not be purely symbolic. Without real efforts to achieve a ceasefire, end the occupation, lift the siege and stop the settlements in the West Bank, it makes no sense,” says the analyst.
Oxfam est présente en Palestine depuis p: Oxfam has been present in Palestine for more than 50 years. It is responding to the humanitarian crisis caused by the Israeli siege of Gaza and works on the ground with partner organizations to provide health services to pregnant women and girls, as well as psychosocial support to displaced people.
« Étant donné que nous menons ces projet: “Given that we run these projects in Palestine, we want to show Canada that it is hypocritical to help us, to support and fund these projects, while fuelling the humanitarian crisis, the genocide and the occupation by supplying weapons to the very people who are occupying the territory,” says Ms<sup>.</sup> Pelletier-Marcotte.
Quoi qu’il en soit, la mission d’Oxfam n: In any case, Oxfam’s mission does not rule out advocacy and applying pressure. “We are working alongside [other organizations] to bring [our] demands to the Canadian government so that it acts in a meaningful way and doesn’t just issue statements of concern,” she says.
En réponse à cette prise de conscience e: In response to this awareness and the escalating violence against Gazans, Oxfam is calling on Canada to take responsibility, end its arms trade, support international justice mechanisms and keep demanding a ceasefire.
La Converse a contacté Anita Anand, mini: La Converse contacted Anita Anand, Canada’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, for comment on the recognition and on Canada’s arms trade with Israel, but she had not responded to the request at the time of publication.
